name: Jordan
headline: Having weight on your back and choosing to bear it translates to resilience
excerpt: More than a decade of training in a public gym, and always yes when friends ask for a hike. Jordan measures strength by whether he stays useful and dependable to the people around him.
q1: Mainly through training at my public gym. I always say yes when friends ask to go for a hike or play other sports. I have been training for over a decade — I started mainly for school sport, but I want to remain useful and dependable for my family and friends.
q2: Strength is about resistance to external pressure, which could be in the weight room, or in life's circumstances. I believe that having weight on your back and choosing to bear it translates over to resilience in other aspects of life.
q3: It's great to see where I can help my friends and family. Convincing my parents to start strength training has been very rewarding for me — they can see life-changing results so quickly.

name: Maddie
headline: I want my children to know I am strong and capable as they grow
excerpt: Two small kids, postgrad study, full-time work, and soccer on weekends. Building strength isn't separate from life — it's woven into it.
q1: I attend Kieser twice a week for assisted training with an exercise scientist, following an individualised program based on my physical needs. I play women's soccer locally and I run. Kieser since 2025, running since 2017, soccer since 2025.
q2: I have two small children and need to be strong to manage domestically. I want to enjoy my hobbies and have the strength and endurance to complete my post grad studies while working full time.
q3: Jayden, my exercise scientist at Kieser, is a key part of my motivation to keep going to training — we swap stories of our children while working on some of my training challenges. I enjoy soccer because it is with local women and we are there for each other in the team. Soccer is new to me so I have needed to learn and everyone has been kind and patient. Friendships in my local community are important to me and weaving these into being and staying strong makes sense. I want my children to know I am strong and capable as they grow into their own lives.

name: Oliver
headline: You sit in the discomfort and find the solution — that's what jiu-jitsu teaches you
excerpt: Brazilian jiu-jitsu since 2021. The mat teaches you to think clearly under pressure, and that translates to every part of life.
q1: I have been doing Brazilian jiu-jitsu since 2021. It makes you strong both physically and mentally as it tests your ability to find solutions in intense, dangerous moments. It also encourages great cardiovascular fitness and conditioning.
q2: Doing jiu-jitsu makes you strong because there are always people who are better than you, so you are never safe from being submitted, pinned down, or controlled. You learn to understand the techniques themselves — you sit in the discomfort of not having control and learn how to relax and find the solution through mental gymnastics. Many thousands of repetitions of the physical side translates into giving you better tools for the mental side.
q3: I have built friends for life — friendships and connections and training partners who support you through all of it, the battle and the tough experiences.

name: Nicole
headline: I'm not sporty — but strength has become fundamental to who I am
excerpt: A spondylolisthesis diagnosis changed everything. Five years at Kieser later, twice-a-week training is just part of how I function as a mother, a lawyer, and a person.
q1: I've been going to Kieser for over five years. I have a spinal condition called spondylolisthesis — my GP referred me to treat it. I've never really been a sporty person, nor have I played team sports. I went to the gym before I had kids, sporadically. Now I go to Kieser twice a week and I walk at least six times a week with the dogs, a few kilometres a day. That helps to grow and maintain my strength.
q2: Physical strength is a big part of being strong, but I think if you're a disabled person or not physically able to be strong, you can still be a strong person. Mental strength and resilience is a big part of being a strong human as well. For me, being physically strong means being able to operate as a mother and a full-time employee. I need to be able to pick up groceries, carry laundry, handle the dogs, have a strong core and generally look after myself and my spondylolisthesis. Physical strength helps me to better deal with the stresses of everyday life — of being a full-time lawyer, of managing a household but also to be able to enjoy life and participate in the activities that I love.
q3: My family motivate me — my two kids, my husband, my dogs. We're an affectionate family who support each other to be healthy. But community is also important. My work community, residential and social community and Kieser community all motivate me to be strong. My family and I live in a little cul-de-sac and we're friendly with our neighbours and watch out for each other. My Kieser team is important in keeping me motivated to maintain my strength. It is very positive, friendly and inviting. When I first started at Kieser, I thought it was mainly for older people, but I soon realised there is a whole age range, from high school students to octogenarians. Now it's become fundamental to who I am — it's really quite crucial, it's just part of my life.

name: Jeffo
headline: I can do things around the house now that I couldn't when I retired
excerpt: One to two hours of walking a day for six years, plus targeted back, knee and arm work. Jeffo measures his strength in stairs climbed, ladders managed and jobs that are no longer out of reach.
q1: Walking 1 to 2 hours a day. Keeping active at home — chores, garage work, errands. Specific back and knee strengthening exercises, and arm exercises. Six years.
q2: Being physically active. Able to work easily, climbing stairs, lifting heavy weights, climbing ladders, completing tasks around the house that I couldn't when I retired.

name: Coralie
headline: Being old doesn't mean diminishment — I want to be a model for my grandchildren
excerpt: Dancing through her fifties, then Kieser from her sixties. Coralie has built a second home at her clinic — and a philosophy for ageing on her own terms.
q1: I decided I needed to build my strength in 2017 and joined Kieser Pymble. I trained intermittently — in my fifties I danced a fair bit and that made me fit and strong, but that reduced in my sixties until I enrolled at Kieser. I didn't do any sport as a kid.
q2: As an older person I want to be a model for my grandchildren and children — that being old doesn't mean diminishment and frailty. I want to be there for them and for other young people. I feel we have lost the art of being older people valued by younger generations and I would like to bring that back.
q3: I call my Kieser Pymble clinic "my second home." On my clinic mornings I am happy to go to training — I look forward to the sessions and the conversations. Jayden is my exercise scientist, Travis is my exercise physiologist (bones and balance classes), and Geordie is my physio who oversees my rehabilitation periodically. I have learned how to manage pain and get strong despite injuries and surgeries. I believe the relationships I have with my clinical team are crucial to my feeling of safety and care. Throughout these conversations I have learned about nutrition — my increased need for protein in particular to avoid muscle loss as I age — and how my nervous system functions through pain and recovery.

name: Judith
headline: Family is first — especially being around to see the grandchildren grow and thrive
excerpt: Ten years of daily walking, sometimes up to ten kilometres. For Judith, strength is about sound mind, community connection, and being a leader in the lives of the people she loves.
q1: I am a daily walker, sometimes up to 10 kilometres a day. I began walking 10 years ago and it is now a part of my life.
q2: Being healthy and of sound mind, having strong connections to my family and community. Being a leader.
q3: Family is first and that can be motivation enough, especially being around to see the grandchildren grow and thrive.

name: Fiona
headline: I need to be strong physically and mentally to support my family, despite ageing
excerpt: Regular walks with her husband and dog Maggie keep Fiona active. Strength, for her, isn't about training — it's about staying capable enough to support her family through everything ahead.
q1: I try to do regular walks with my husband and our dog Maggie. It's not really structured training — I'm just aware of the ageing process and the need to remain strong and active.
q2: I want to be able to support my family through all aspects of life, so I need to be strong physically and mentally to do that well despite ageing.
q3: Mostly my close family — they encourage me toward more social activities and keep me motivated to stay active.

name: Peter
headline: My five grandchildren know I stay strong — and I want to keep it that way
excerpt: Cycling since his early fifties, Kieser since 2024. Peter's strength is as much about community and human kindness as it is about physical capacity.
q1: I have participated in group cycling activity since my early fifties and still do. More recently I have attended Kieser twice a week for individual assisted machine-based strength training, and I participate in a balance class. Kieser since 2024, cycling since 2005.
q2: I have five grandchildren and I like them to know I am strong and invest in staying strong for them. I like to be able to look after our home and be able to do physical activities as part of my domestic and social life. I also think that being strong involves being active in my community.
q3: I have a great community related to cycling. We have developed friendships — we all help each other when needed. I look forward to my Kieser sessions as the young professionals there genuinely support me with their knowledge and human kindness. We share details of our lives and I feel a part of a strong Kieser community as well.
